title: The Greeks by shape
objectives: Sketch delta, gamma, vega and theta against spot and time, and sign them for common positions.
Get vega and theta from gamma and net the Greeks of a position

screens.title: Sketch the delta
screens.prose: Interviewer: sketch the delta of an at-the-money call, then tell me its gamma, vega and theta from the picture. Start with delta. One year left, $r = 0$.
screens.question: Drag the five points to sketch the call's delta against spot.

hints.text: Far below the strike, how much of the share does the option act like?
At the money the share could go either way, but a little more up than down.
Start near 0 at £60, about 0.54 at £100 (not 0.5), and end near 1 at £140.

feedback.correct: An S-shape from 0 to 1, with 0.54 at the strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Delta runs from 0 to 1 and passes about 0.54 at the strike.

byKey.ramp: You drew a straight ramp. Delta flattens at both ends and is steepest at the strike.

explain.text: Delta is $\Phi(d_1)$: near 0 deep out of the money, 0.5398 at the strike and near 1 deep in. It sits just above 0.5 because $d_1 = 0.1$. The steepest part is at the strike.

screens.title: Where is gamma biggest?
screens.prose: Gamma is delta's slope. The dashed curve is delta and the bold curve is gamma × 100. Same option, one year left.
screens.question: Drag the point to the peak of gamma.

hints.text: Where is delta changing fastest?
Gamma is large where the dashed curve is steepest.
The peak is a little left of £100, near £94.

feedback.correct: The peak is at £94.18, a little left of the strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the dashed delta curve is steepest.

byKey.deep-itm: You put the peak where delta is flat. Gamma is delta's slope.
byKey.deep-otm: You put the peak where delta is flat. Gamma is delta's slope.
byKey.at-strike: The peak is a little left of the strike, because the share's moves are proportional.
byKey.p1: That is not the highest point of the bold curve. Look for where the dashed delta curve is steepest.

explain.text: Gamma peaks at $100e^{-1.5\sigma^2T} = 94.18$, where it is 0.02076, against 0.01985 at the strike. The peak is broad, so the strike is a fair guess.

screens.title: Gamma as expiry nears
screens.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. Slide through four expiries. Bold is gamma × 100 for the strike 100. Dashed is the same for a call struck at 130. The point sits at spot £100 on the dashed curve.

state.caption: σ = 20%, r = 0. Read the point's value at each expiry.

screens.question: For the call struck at 130, gamma at spot £100 with $T = 1$ is how many times gamma with $T = 0.25$?

feedback.correct: Far from the strike, more time means more gamma.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the point's value at one year and at three months, then divide.

byKey.atm-habit: You used the at-the-money habit, that gamma falls with time. Far out of the money it rises with time.
byKey.same: You kept gamma the same. Slide the control: the point's value changes a lot.

explain.text: At the strike gamma goes as $1/\sqrt T$: the bold curve narrows and rises, reaching 14.4 one week out. Far from the strike it goes the other way. Gamma is 0.009572 at one year and 0.001454 at three months, a ratio of 6.6.

screens.title: Vega from gamma
screens.prose: New identity: vega $= \Gamma S^2\sigma T$ per 1.00 of vol. The picture is the vega curve per vol point. At $S = 100$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$, gamma is 0.0198.
screens.question: What is vega per vol point at the strike?

widget.label: Vega per vol point in pounds

hints.text: Put the numbers into $\Gamma S^2\sigma T$.
That gives vega for a move of 1.00 in vol. A vol point is 0.01.
$0.0198 \times 10{,}000 \times 0.2 = 39.6$, so about £0.40 a point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\Gamma S^2\sigma T$, then divide by 100 for one vol point.

byKey.per-unit: You stopped at 39.7, the vega for a move of 1.00 in vol. A vol point is 0.01 of that.
byKey.no-sigma: You left out the vol in $\Gamma S^2\sigma T$. It must be there to give 39.7.

explain.text: $\Gamma S^2\sigma T = 0.0198 \times 10{,}000 \times 0.2 \times 1 = 39.6$, and the exact gamma gives 39.695. One vol point is £0.397, the same as the rule of thumb's £0.40.

screens.title: Theta from gamma
screens.prose: Pushed one step: at $r = 0$ theta follows from gamma, $\Theta = -\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$ a year. The picture is theta per trading day. Gamma is still 0.0198 at $S = 100$, $\sigma = 20\%$.
screens.question: What is theta per trading day (252 a year)?

hints.text: Put the numbers into the identity, then divide by the trading days.
Do not forget the half.
$-\tfrac12 \times 0.04 \times 10{,}000 \times 0.0198 = -3.96$ a year; $\div 252$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $-\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$, then divide by 252.

byKey.year: You gave the year's theta. A trading day is 1/252 of it.
byKey.no-half: You left out the half in $-\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$.
byKey.sign: A long option pays theta each day, so theta is negative: −3.96/252 is about −£0.0157. A positive £0.0158 books the daily decay as a gain.

explain.text: Theta a year is $-\tfrac12 \times 0.04 \times 10{,}000 \times 0.0198 = -3.96$, so −£0.0157 a day with this gamma and −£0.01575 exactly. Gamma and theta trade off: a long option pays theta for gamma.

screens.title: Signs of three positions
screens.prose: Collect the signs, all at the money with $r = 0$. Type +, − or 0, where 0 means about zero. A straddle is a call and a put. A calendar sells the 1-month call and buys the 3-month call.
screens.question: Fill in the sign of each Greek for each position (one column each).

hints.text: Start with the straddle: the call's delta and the put's delta.
A calendar is long the slow option and short the sharp one: compare their gammas.
Straddle: 0, +, +, −. Calendar: 0, −, +, +. Short call: all flipped except theta.

feedback.correct: A long straddle buys movement; a calendar sells gamma and buys vega.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the legs' Greeks and flip the signs of what you sold.

byKey.r1c1: A short call has negative gamma: it loses on big moves.
byKey.r0c2: A straddle's delta is about 0: the call's and the put's cancel.
byKey.r1c3: You sold the 1-month call, which has the larger gamma, so the net gamma is negative.
byKey.r3c3: You sell the faster decay and buy the slower one, so the net theta is positive.

explain.text: Net for the calendar: delta 0.0084, gamma −0.0292, vega +0.0841 a point and theta +£0.0232 a day. The 1-month gamma is 0.0691 against 0.0398 for 3 months. A straddle is long gamma and vega and pays theta.

screens.title: More time, more gamma
screens.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. A candidate says: a long-dated option has more time, so it has more gamma. The curves are the at-the-money gamma × 100 for $T = 1$ and $T = 0.25$.
screens.question: Which statement is right at the strike?

options.text: Gamma falls with time left, as $1/\sqrt T$, while vega rises, as $\sqrt T$
The candidate is right: more time gives more chances to cross the strike
options.why: You counted chances to cross the strike. Gamma is how sharply delta changes, and long-dated delta changes slowly.

options.text: Gamma and vega both rise with time
options.why: You gave gamma vega's shape. Vega rises with $\sqrt T$, but gamma falls.

options.text: Gamma is the same at the strike for every $T$
options.why: You assumed gamma depends only on the strike. At the money it is 0.0198 at one year and 0.0398 at three months.

hints.text: Compare the two peaks.
The dashed curve, with less time, is taller and narrower.
Gamma at the strike goes as $1/\sqrt T$; vega goes as $\sqrt T$.

feedback.correct: Short-dated options have the sharp, high gamma at the strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the heights of the two peaks.

byKey.more: You counted chances. Compare the heights of the curves instead.
byKey.both: Gamma and vega go in opposite directions in time: 0.0398 against 0.0198 for gamma.
byKey.same: The curves have different heights at the strike.

explain.text: At the strike gamma is 0.0198 at one year and 0.0398 at three months, a ratio of 2.0075. Vega is 0.397 against 0.199 a point, a ratio of 0.5019. Far from the strike the order of gamma reverses, as the last screen showed.

screens.title: One day to expiry
screens.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. Edge case. The curves are gamma × 100 for one year and for one trading day, $T = 1/252$, both at the money.
screens.question: How many times is gamma at the strike one day from expiry against one year?

hints.text: Use how gamma scales with time at the strike.
One day is 1/252 of a year.

feedback.correct: About 16 times, because gamma goes as $1/\sqrt T$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. At the strike gamma goes as $1/\sqrt T$.

byKey.linear: You scaled by $1/T$, giving 252. Gamma goes as $1/\sqrt T$, so the ratio is $\sqrt{252}$.
byKey.same: You kept gamma the same. One day from expiry delta is nearly a step, so gamma is far larger.

explain.text: The gamma is 0.3166 against 0.0198, a ratio of 15.95. Delta becomes a step, so gamma blows up at the strike.

screens.title: A desk's theta bleed
screens.prose: Interviewer: a desk is long 10,000 three-month at-the-money straddles. $S = 100$, vol 20%, $r = 0$. About 90 seconds: say the sign, then the number. Each straddle has theta −15.94 a year.
screens.question: What is the desk's theta for one trading day?

hints.text: Convert a year of theta to a day, then scale to 10,000.
Divide −15.94 by 252.

feedback.correct: The desk bleeds about £632 a day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One straddle's theta a day, times 10,000.

byKey.year: You did not divide by 252. That is the whole year's theta.
byKey.one-leg: You counted one leg, the call. A straddle has two, and their thetas add.
byKey.sign: The desk is long straddles, which lose value each day, so theta is −£632.45. A positive 632 books the daily decay as a gain.

explain.text: Theta is −£632.45 a day: a straddle's theta is twice a call's. Say aloud: it earns that back only if the share moves more than about £1.26 a day. Lesson 18 derives that breakeven move.

screens.title: The Greeks in code
screens.prose: Interviewer: now do it for a book. `bs_greeks` takes gamma from $d_1$ and gets vega and theta from the two identities. `net_greeks` adds signed legs. Give a short position a negative `qty`. Reading, once for the level: Hull's Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives covers the Greeks and exotics. Joshi's Quant Job Interview Questions and Answers collects questions like these.

state.caption: The calendar's two legs, σ = 20%, r = 0.

screens.question: Complete `bs_greeks` and `net_greeks`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, including the calendar and the straddle, compared with `math.isclose` to 4 places.

hints.text: Start with $\Phi(d_1)$ for delta and the density for gamma.
Vega and theta need only gamma, $S$, $\sigma$ and $T$.
For a put, subtract 1 from delta, then scale every Greek by `qty`.

feedback.correct: Your function reproduces the calendar and the straddle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the divisions by 100 and 252, and that a put's delta is the call's minus 1.

explain.text: The calendar nets to delta 0.0084, gamma −0.0292, vega 0.0841 and theta 0.0232: short gamma, long vega, paid theta. Round only at the end, or the fourth place drifts.

ideas: Delta is an S-shaped curve from 0 to 1. Gamma is its slope and peaks just below the strike.
At the strike gamma goes as $1/\sqrt T$ and vega as $\sqrt T$; far from the strike gamma rises with $T$.
At $r = 0$, vega $= \Gamma S^2\sigma T$ and $\Theta = -\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$, so one number, gamma, gives the other two.

formula.name: Gamma, vega and theta
formula.note: r = 0, at the money, per 1.00 of vol and per year.

summary.trap: More time does not mean more gamma at the strike: it means less, and more vega.

quiz.prose: You are short one at-the-money call and have not hedged.
quiz.question: What is the sign of your gamma?

options.text: Negative: you lose on big moves in either direction
Positive: the call's price curve bends upwards
options.why: You read the long call's curve. Being short flips gamma to negative.

options.text: Zero: delta is fixed by the strike
options.why: You treated delta as fixed. Delta moves with the share, and gamma is that rate of change.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A short position has the long position's signs flipped.

explain.text: A long call's gamma is positive, and a short call has the opposite sign. The short call loses more the further the share moves.

quiz.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. An at-the-money option, $r = 0$, as expiry approaches with the share at the strike.
quiz.question: Which Greek gets smaller?

options.why: You carried the long-dated picture. Gamma rises as expiry nears.

options.text: Theta's size, which goes as $1/\sqrt T$
options.why: You assumed decay slows. At the money it speeds up as expiry nears.

feedback.correct: Only vega falls: less time means less sensitivity to vol.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Gamma and the size of theta grow at the strike.

explain.text: Vega is 39.70 at one year and 2.51 one day out. Gamma and theta both grow as $1/\sqrt T$ at the strike.

quiz.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. An at-the-money call, strike 100, with the share at £100 and $r = 0$.
quiz.question: How does its gamma change as expiry nears?

options.why: You gave gamma vega's shape. Gamma rises as the delta curve steepens.
You ignored time. The delta curve gets steeper at the strike as expiry nears.

feedback.correct: Gamma at the strike rises as expiry nears.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Delta becomes a step at expiry.

explain.text: Gamma is 0.0198 at one year, 0.0398 at three months and 0.3166 one day out.

quiz.prose: Recall from the options course, lesson 14. You are long an at-the-money straddle, $r = 0$.
quiz.question: What is the sign of its theta, and how does it compare with a call's?

options.why: You carried delta's cancellation over. Theta adds across the legs.

options.text: Positive, since you hold two options
options.why: You treated two options as two sources of income. Long options pay theta.

feedback.correct: The legs' thetas are equal and add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Long options pay time decay.

explain.text: At $r = 0$ a call and a put share one theta, so the straddle's is twice a call's. For three months that is −£15.94 a year.
